The book titled, ‘Mountains of Our Destiny: The Western Ghats, A Journey Through The Southern Monsoon Mountains by Vrinda Ramanan and J. Ramanan is a sequel to ‘Mountains of our Destiny: An Expedition to the Indian Himalaya’, also by the same authors.

The Hindu launched a coffee table book titled, ‘Mountains of Our Destiny: The Western Ghats, A Journey Through The Southern Monsoon Mountains’, on Wednesday (November 25, 2026). Authored by Vrinda Ramanan and J. Ramanan, mountaineers, writers and photographers, the book was launched by Tamil Nadu Forests Minister R.V. Ranjith Kumar. The first copies were received by Rohit Ramesh, Director, Suresh Nambath, Editor, and L.V. Navaneeth, CEO, The Hindu . The book is a sequel to ‘Mountains of our Destiny: An Expedition to the Indian Himalaya’, also by the same authors.

Speaking on the occasion, the Minister noted the importance of the forests, rivers and mountains to sustaining agriculture, livelihoods and ecological balance. He highlighted the need to ensure forest conservation, spoke of the measures taken by the government to improve upon work being done, such as AI technology to prevent elephant deaths on railway tracks and in the control of forest fires, and congratulated the authors on their work.

Author J. Ramanan explained that the two mountain ranges: the Himalayas and the Western Ghats formed the bedrock of India’s existence. Without them, he said, we would not have had our rivers. The 1,500 km Western Ghats in particular, recognised as a biodiversity hotspot, was one of the richest ecological resources in the country, sustaining thousands of lives. The monsoon in India, Mr. Ramanan said, is shaped by the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. The book was an attempt to create awareness about, and educate people on the importance of maintaining ecological balance through their preservation.

Through more than 400 photographs, field experiences and narratives, the book explores the geology, wildlife, plants, indigenous communities and the intricate web of life that sustains these mountains. It also examines the growing pressures of plantations, invasive species, tourism, dams and other human interventions, highlighting the urgent need for conservation.

The book is available at The Hindu ’s online bookstore: https://publications.thehindugroup.com/ . The cover price of the book is ₹2,999. articles.title: J&K clerics apologise, offer ‘repentance prayers’ for standing during Vande Mataram at Waqf Board function
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: After Vande Mataram was played at the first Waqf Day function, clerics say they recited the ‘kalima’ in repentance; Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulama may seek legal opinion

A group of prominent Muslim clerics who attended the Waqf Day function in Srinagar on Monday (November 23, 2026) apologised on Wednesday and “offered repentance prayers” over standing during the Vande Mataram song, as the incident triggered a wave of protests from religious groups in J&K, including the Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU).

The controversy was sparked by the November 23 event of the J&K Waqf Board that was attended by Union Minority Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology, Srinagar. At the first-ever Waqf Day function organised by BJP leader and J&K Waqf Board chairperson Darakhshan Andrabi, the full Vande Mataram song was played with several top Muslim clerics on the dais as well as in the audience. National Conference (NC) MP Mian Altaf Larvi and Shia cleric and J&K Peoples Conference leader Imran Reza Ansari also attended the function.

Facing criticism, Maulana Farooq, accompanied by other clerics, said in an online video, “Some things unacceptable from the Sharia point of view took place on the occasion. We repent for the same. We went outside the venue, immediately recited ‘ kalima ’ in a congregation and offered our repentance. Ulemas from other sects also attended it. We did not recite anything from our hearts. Allah will accept our repentance.”

Those who attended the function included Mufti Syed Basharat, Mufti Farooq, Mufti Inayatullah Qasmi, Maulana Farooq, Maulana Basharat Sakafi, Pir Syed Ejaz, Maulana Zakir, Abdul Rashid Dawoodi and imams of the Dastigeer Sahib shrine and the Hazratbal shrine.

Maulana Rahmatullah, who heads Kashmir’s biggest seminary, Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, welcomed the “act of repentance by the Muslim priests for their mistake”. “I congratulate these religious leaders for their immediate repentance prayers and reciting the ‘kalima’ again for the mistake. Allah must be pleased with them.”

Mr. Rahmatullah said anything that interferes with the faith of Muslims “is not acceptable”. “Mr. Dawoodi should have mentioned the Supreme Court ruling and clarified that the Vande Mataram cannot be forced. It was not a political stage but a Waqf function. I had advised Ms. Andrabi beforehand that you belong to a family who have spread Islam. I fail to understand why she committed this wrong. She should have conveyed to sing Jana Gana Mana but not play with religious sentiments and sing Vande Mataram . I ask Mr. Dawoodi to educate Ms. Andrabi on this, but then granting ‘ imaan ’ is in the hands of Allah,” said Mr. Rahmatullah.

Meanwhile, the MMU, an amalgam of religious organisations headed by Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, said, “It has categorically made clear on several occasions in the past, the fundamental and non-negotiable principle of Tawheed in Islam — the absolute Oneness of Allah. Islam strictly prohibits associating any partner with Allah or attributing divinity to any person, object, land or creation.”

The MMU said it was highly “regrettable and unacceptable” that Vande Mataram was played at the function of the Waqf Board, an institution entrusted with safeguarding Muslim religious endowments and their sanctity. “There was no legal obligation to play Vande Mataram simply because it was an official function, and playing it was optional,” said the MMU.
It said the Waqf Board went ahead “with utter disregard for the fundamental religious beliefs and sensitivities of Kashmiri Muslims, which has caused deep hurt and anguish among people.”

“The MMU expresses grave concern over the increasingly routine inclusion of Vande Mataram at official government functions across Muslim-majority Jammu and Kashmir, despite the well-known religious reservations of Muslims. Such imposition disregards their religious convictions and constitutional rights and deepens distrust and alienation,” said the MMU spokesman.

articles.title: Air passenger services see 35% inflation in Q2; banking, securities transaction witness deflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The Commerce and Industry Ministry released the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27

Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.
The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.
Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.
As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.
Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.
Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.
Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.
The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

The Commerce and Industry Ministry released the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27

Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.

The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.

Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.

As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.

Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.

Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.

Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.

The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

articles.title: Global climate talks must shut door on fossil fuel ‘clout’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The breakdown in the Antalya summit has deepened the crisis of confidence in climate diplomacy, making transparency and accountability in the negotiating process more urgent than ever.

The failure of the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to agree on its central political statement, with countries unable to bridge their differences over fossil fuels and other key questions of climate action, has exposed the fragility of international climate cooperation. It should also sharpen scrutiny of who gets access to climate negotiations, whose interests they represent and what safeguards keep decisions accountable to the public.

The Türkiye summit ended without agreement on an overarching statement. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

The breakdown does not show that fossil fuel lobbying caused the impasse. But it does make more urgent a separate question about the credibility of the process. A forum that asks governments to make decisions in the global public interest must be transparent about who is seeking to shape those decisions, what interests they represent and how conflicts are managed.

The international climate negotiations that take place every year still lack a comprehensive, enforceable system to identify and manage conflicts of interest involving powerful commercial interests, including fossil fuel companies and state-owned energy businesses. The Antalya conference has underlined why that gap matters.

The fossil fuel industry’s record of muddying the waters is well documented. A 2017 study by Geoffrey Supran and Naomi Oreskes compared 187 ExxonMobil communications between 1977 and 2014, including internal documents, scientific publications and paid newspaper advertorials. It found that as the company’s communications became more public, they increasingly expressed doubt about climate science. The researchers concluded that ExxonMobil had contributed to climate science while promoting doubt about it in its advertorials.

An industry team discussed a 1998 draft of the Global Climate Science Communications Plan at the American Petroleum Institute’s headquarters. The plan’s stated goal was to persuade a majority of the American public that significant uncertainties remained in climate science and to raise questions among policymakers.

This history matters because companies with large investments in oil, gas and coal have a financial stake in how quickly those fuels are phased down, which technologies receive support and how the costs of the transition are distributed. That does not mean every company representative at a climate summit is there to obstruct progress, or that attendance proves influence over a decision. It, however, does mean commercial interests need to be visible and the process needs rules to prevent undue influence.

The scale of corporate participation in Antalya brings the issue into sharper focus. An analysis by a coalition of non-profits identified 103 major polluter groups with delegations at the summit, including fossil fuel businesses, financiers and companies from other high-emitting sectors. It also identified 30 banks whose fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025 amounted to more than $2.2 trillion.

These are the coalition’s classifications, not official UN figures. They do not establish that the companies or banks influenced the negotiations. But they show the scale of commercial interests present at a conference whose purpose is to limit global warming.

Lien Vandamme of the Center for International Environmental Law says the problem goes beyond the number of corporate participants. Although the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has introduced limited disclosure requirements, she argues that it still lacks a policy to curb corporate influence. “There is currently no policy to curb corporate influence within the UNFCCC process, and this is a fundamental problem,” she says. Once companies gain access, she argues, it becomes extremely difficult to monitor how they use it to influence negotiations.

articles.title: UK police charge two men over a break-in at Prince William and Princess Catherine’s country home
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II
Two men have been charged with burglary at the country home of Prince William and Princess Catherine, police said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

The Norfolk Police force says Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They are due in court later on Wednesday.

Police officers were called on Monday evening to reported “suspicious activity” at an address on the royal family's rural Sandringham estate in eastern England. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.
William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office declined to comment on security matters.
Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II.

William and Kate use the secluded red brick Georgian mansion about 110 miles (171 kilometres) north of London as a country residence on weekends. The couple and their three children spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, west of London, which they have described as their “forever home.”
Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. Charles and Queen Camilla weren’t at Windsor Castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Kate were in their nearby house.

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

articles.title: At least two Indians among 11 injured in Houthi attack in Riyadh; New Delhi condemns strike
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence said a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District came under what it described as a "terrorist attack" by Houthi militia
Two Indians were among those injured in an attack on a financial district in Riyadh that triggered strong condemnation from New Delhi.
India also denounced continued strikes targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

“Two Indians are among those injured in the attack on Riyadh financial district. The embassy of India in Riyadh is providing all possible assistance to the injured and their families,” the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said.
The attack was carried out on Tuesday (November 24, 2026). Local authorities said the injured included two Saudi citizens, three Nepalese and four Egyptian nationals.

The MEA said India strongly condemns the attack in Riyadh as well as the continued strikes targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. “These attacks seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability. We call for immediate cessation of such attacks,” it said in a statement.

India also reiterated its firm solidarity with the people and government of Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its unwavering support to the Kingdom in safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
“We earnestly hope that peace and normalcy will return to the region at the earliest,” the MEA said.
There has been a sudden escalation in tensions in West Asia, especially after the Houthis carried out several strikes on Saudi Arabia.
The West Asia conflict began in February following attacks on Iran by the U.S. and Israel. New Delhi has consistently called for finding a solution to the conflict through dialogue and diplomacy.

India has been specifically voicing serious concern over the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s civilian infrastructure and economic assets, cautioning that such strikes undermine regional stability and threaten freedom of navigation through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.

articles.title: Meet the little stint: The tiny Siberian traveller visiting India’s wetlands
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Little Stint travels thousands of kilometres between its Arctic breeding grounds and Indian wetlands. But as shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands

The little stint, a 25-gram shorebird, comes in lakhs from the Arctic to the shores of India, particularly to Point Calimere. “It’s an unforgettable sight,” says S Sivakumar, who has been involved in monitoring shorebirds in the Gulf of Mannar for over a decade. The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May. “In the 1980s, the little stint could be seen in several lakhs at any point of time. Even now, the numbers are still over a lakh as the Point Calimere Wetland Complex covers over 300 kilometres across coastal Tamil Nadu ,” says Sivakumar, assistant director at the Bombay Natural History Society’s Bird Migration Study Centre at Point Calimere, adding that such long-term observations help scientists understand how bird populations and their habitats are changing.
The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May | Photo Credit: S Sivakumar

The tiny bird’s annual migration journey, a feat of endurance, involves multiple stopovers across different landscapes, each of which must provide sufficient food and safe resting grounds. As shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands.

Ashvin Viswanathan, scientist at Bird Count India , places the little stints as the most visible representatives of a special group of shorebirds that breed in the Arctic. “ This group is declining rapidly due to climate change and loss of habitat. Little stints too are declining in India according to SoIB,” he says, referring to the State of India’s Birds assessment. Their widespread presence, he adds, indicates the health of wetland ecosystems in India as well as conditions in the Arctic. The fact that the little stint is still a fairly common bird does not mean that it is beyond risk. It’s numbers and distribution can help draw attention to changes taking place across the habitats it depends on.
The numbers are still over a lakh at Point Calimere wetlands | Photo Credit: S Sivakumar

The bird’s preparation for migration is as fascinating as the journey itself. “Before setting off, they enter a phase of intense feeding called hyperphagia. They feed voraciously to build up fat reserves that act as fuel during its journey.

This can add 50 to 75 percent to the bird’s body weight. There are also physiological changes, some organs shrink in size as the bird prepares for the demands of sustained flight,” explains Sivakumar adding that India is an important destination along the Central Asian Flyway that connects the bird with wintering habitats further South. The birds can be found along several coastal wetlands, including Point Calimere, Pulicat, parts of Puducherry and Kanyakumari, the Sundarbans, and the mudflats of Gujarat and Maharashtra. Across Tamil Nadu, the species is familiar to birders. “You can spot them at wetlands such as Kurichi and Ukkadam in Coimbatore,” says birder K Selvaganesh adding that the flock plays an important part of the food chain as prey for raptors, including the Western marsh marrier and the brahminy kite.

Goa-based Rakesh Dhareshwar, a wildlife photographer says Goa and the wider west coast are reliable places to find them each season. “This year, I was delighted to see them inland too, at Bhigwan in Maharashtra, during a mid-Novemeber trip. However, shorebirds worldwide are in decline. Loss of coastal and inland wetlands, reclamation of mudflats, and pollution threaten stopover and wintering sites these birds depend on. The good news is that we can fix this. Protecting wetlands, salt pans and estuaries, and sharing spaces thoughtfully with people can make a real difference.”
Shorebirds worldwide are in decline | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

In his new book, Little Stint: A Migrant’s Tale (Neythal Pathipakam), author Byju H explores the bird’s remarkable journey through a blend of science and unconventional storytelling allowing the bird to narrate its own life, beginning with emerging from an egg in the Arctic tundra. “I wanted readers to travel with the bird,” he says adding that the book also highlights the fact that the bird’s ability to navigate vast distances depends on the availability of suitable wetlands along its migratory route.

articles.title: Wildlife, forests, and culture in Gudalur: Sculptures, stories, and interactive workshops
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Into the Forest, an ongoing exhibition in Gudalur explores the relationship between forests, wildlife and people through sculptures, stories, workshops for children and creative artefacts made using invasive plant species

What if the plants choking the forests of the Nilgiris could be given a second life as works of art?An ongoing exhibition in Gudalur hopes to tell that story, bringing together conservation, craftsmanship and narratives of the intimate relationship between people and the natural world. “For all of us, sharing space with wildlife is part of everyday life,” says Rhea Antony, who takes care of storytelling and design at The Elephant People, a social enterprise based in Gudalur in the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve that makes hand-carved wildlife sculptures, masks, and everyday objects from invasive plant species like Lantana camara and Senna spectabilis.
Handcrafted objects made using invasive species vegetation | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

The exhibition is an attempt to draw attention to the changing landscapes of the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve, where the invasive species have spread across native habitats. These fast-growing plants suppress native vegetation, particularly grasses, affecting the food sources of wildlife and sometimes pushing animals towards human settlements.
ALSO WATCH Watch: How communities are rebuilding the Nilgiris ecosystem

The Elephant People collective works with Forest Departments of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka in clearing these invasive species. Instead of treating the recovered vegetation as waste, they transform the wood into handcrafted objects and sculptures inspired by the region’s wildlife, people, and landscapes.
The team includes over 50 makers across carving, painting, design, production, and operations | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Titled Into the Forest, the first exhibition by The Elephant People features stories of wildlife, people, shared landscapes, and practices connected to the land. “These stories are brought to life through art and craft, with sculptures and installations created by a team of makers from the Nilgiris, for whom sharing space with wildlife is part of everyday life,” says Rhea. The exhibition features large-scale sculptures, smaller carved pieces, and interactive storytelling experiences. For children, there will be facilitated painting and story-building workshops, alongside interactive art installations that let them explore the forest through play. These installations offer opportunities to learn about different species, their habitats, and the sounds they make.

“Over the last three years, we’ve been exploring the stories of the Nilgiris and finding ways to bring them to life through art and craft. The region has been central to this journey. It’s wildlife, landscapes, people and the many relationships between them have shaped the stories we are drawn to and the work we create ,” says Rhea. While discovering stories of different species, they also learnt about encounters between people and wildlife, traditional practices, food cultures and ways of living that keep the forest at the centre. Some came from conversations with people, others from naturalists and researchers, and many from simply observing the fascinating relationships that exist within these landscapes.
ALSO WATCH Watch: A day at Baralikadu: Coracles, tribal food and community-led tourism
There are smaller objects like magnets and key-chains to large-scale sculptures and interactive installations | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

articles.title: When public duty meets medical privacy
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A legislator undergoing prolonged treatment may retain the ability to perform official responsibilities. Functional capacity, rather than diagnosis alone, is therefore central to the legal question of what the public has the right to know

Sonia Gandhi, in her recently published memoir, recalls being advised surgery for suspected breast cancer in 2010. Since she is a prominent public figure, she wonders, in her book, whether she was entitled to even a modicum of privacy with regard to her health. Her account assumes renewed significance following a recent petition before the Madras High Court that inquired about the health of Kolathur MLA V.S. Babu (now deceased). These episodes expose a fundamental legal tension between the privacy politicians may want about their health, and the accountability they owe their constituents in a democracy. Does the public’s right to information justify waiving or limiting an office-holder’s medical confidentiality? How should a democracy reconcile these competing interests?

Medical information is among the most sensitive forms of personal information. A diagnosis may reveal not merely someone’s present condition but also their reproductive history, genetic predispositions, psychiatric illness or future health risks. Disclosure can invite discrimination, political exploitation and public speculation. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. Holding public office does not automatically extinguish this protection. A politician receiving treatment need not publish laboratory reports. Nor does a disability establish an inability to govern. State intrusion needs lawful justification, not curiosity.

The Constitution does not prescribe a general medical-fitness requirement for occupying high public office. Article 58 sets eligibility conditions for the President but requires no medical-fitness certificate. Article 65(2) allows the Vice-President to perform presidential functions when the President cannot do so through absence, illness or another cause. The Constitution recognises presidential illness but does not specify a detailed procedure or medical authority to determine contested incapacity. This distinction between eligibility to assume office and capacity to continue functioning deserves closer scrutiny.

For legislators, Articles 102 and 191 prescribe disqualification when a person is of ‘unsound mind’ and stands so declared by a competent court (not by a medical board). Section 16(1)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, similarly provides for disqualification from electoral registration (by court not medical board). For Supreme Court judges, Article 124(4) permits removal on proof of incapacity, while the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, provides a procedure that may involve a Medical Board. Article 317(3)(c), governing Public Service Commission members, permits removal for unfitness arising from ‘infirmity of mind or body’.

articles.title: The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too

In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

Modern governance, however, forgot what Ashoka and Virchow knew. It allotted people to one ministry, livestock to another and forests to a third, and pathogens, which recognise no such allocation of business, have exploited the gaps ever since. One Health, which the world marks on November 3, is the effort to recover that lost unity with the tools of the 21st century by bringing human, animal and environmental health into a common framework for research, surveillance and prevention. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , which regards the world as one family, resonates with this understanding of interconnected life.

This year the case makes itself. Lumpy skin disease (LSD) has returned to India. The September forecast from ICAR-National Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology and Disease Informatics’ early-warning system placed 219 districts across 28 states and Union Territories at risk, and Rajasthan had recorded more than 10,400 cases in 10 eastern districts by mid-September. In Siberia, a young technician at Irkutsk’s anti-plague institute died in early October, of what Russian authorities called pneumonia of unknown cause, amid reports of pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 people were placed under observation. Whatever the final diagnosis, Yersinia pestis , the organism of the Black Death, has never left us. It persists in rodents and their fleas, from the marmots of the Central Asian steppe to the prairie dogs of New Mexico and the rats of Madagascar.

Neither story respects a departmental boundary. LSD does not infect people, but it drains milk cans, household incomes and children’s nutrition. Plague is at once a problem of wildlife ecology, laboratory biosafety, clinical medicine and public trust.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment 📅 25 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention

🎯 Exam Relevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too

In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

Modern governance, however, forgot what Ashoka and Virchow knew. It allotted people to one ministry, livestock to another and forests to a third, and pathogens, which recognise no such allocation of business, have exploited the gaps ever since. One Health, which the world marks on November 3, is the effort to recover that lost unity with the tools of the 21st century by bringing human, animal and environmental health into a common framework for research, surveillance and prevention. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , which regards the world as one family, resonates with this understanding of interconnected life.

This year the case makes itself. Lumpy skin disease (LSD) has returned to India. The September forecast from ICAR-National Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology and Disease Informatics’ early-warning system placed 219 districts across 28 states and Union Territories at risk, and Rajasthan had recorded more than 10,400 cases in 10 eastern districts by mid-September. In Siberia, a young technician at Irkutsk’s anti-plague institute died in early October, of what Russian authorities called pneumonia of unknown cause, amid reports of pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 people were placed under observation. Whatever the final diagnosis, Yersinia pestis , the organism of the Black Death, has never left us. It persists in rodents and their fleas, from the marmots of the Central Asian steppe to the prairie dogs of New Mexico and the rats of Madagascar.

Neither story respects a departmental boundary. LSD does not infect people, but it drains milk cans, household incomes and children’s nutrition. Plague is at once a problem of wildlife ecology, laboratory biosafety, clinical medicine and public trust.

articles.title: Andhra’s revenue rises 18.7% to ₹74,342 crore; Naidu asks officials to raise more without burdening people
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The State has achieved 58% of its annual own-revenue target of ₹1,27,506 crore, officials tell the Chief Minister

Andhra Pradesh’s own revenue increased by 18.7% to ₹74,342 crore as on November 23 in the 2026-27 financial year, registering an additional collection of ₹11,738 crore compared with the corresponding period last year.

The State has achieved 58% of its annual own-revenue target of ₹1,27,506 crore, officials told Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu during a review meeting on revenue-generating departments on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Mr. Naidu asked officials to improve government revenues without imposing an additional tax burden on people or increasing existing charges. Administrative reforms, transparency, online services and measures to plug revenue leakages had begun yielding results over the past two-and-a-half years. The departments should focus on improving revenue collections every week, analyse the performance and make necessary corrections to achieve better results. All departments should use artificial intelligence (AI) and a dedicated AI stack to identify revenue leakages and improve collections, he said.

ప్రభుత్వానికి ఆదాయం సమకూర్చే శాఖలపై గౌరవ ముఖ్యమంత్రి శ్రీ నారా చంద్రబాబునాయుడు నేడు ఉన్నత స్థాయి సమీక్ష నిర్వహించారు. ఈ సమావేశానికి రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వ ప్రధాన కార్యదర్శి శ్రీ సాయి ప్రసాద్, ఆర్ధిక, రెవెన్యూ, ఎక్సైజ్, స్టాంపులు రిజిస్ట్రేషన్లు, గనులు, రవాణా, పురపాలక, పంచాయితీరాజ్ శాఖల ఉన్నతాధికారులు హాజరయ్యారు. ప్రభుత్వం తీసుకున్న చర్యల ద్వారా లీకేజీలు తగ్గడం, వ్యవస్థీకృత లోపాలను సరిదిద్దడంతో ఆయా శాఖల్లో మెరుగైన ఫలితాలు వచ్చాయని ఈ సందర్భంగా సీఎం తెలిపారు. రాష్ట్రంలో వివిధ ప్రాంతాల్లో జరుగుతున్న అభివృద్ధి కార్యక్రమాల ఫలితాలు ఆదాయంలో ప్రతిఫలించాలని, పన్నుల భారం లేకుండా, కొత్తగా ఛార్జీలు పెంచకుండా వివిధ ప్రభుత్వ శాఖల్లో ఆదాయం పెంచేందుకు కృషి చేయాలని అధికారులను ఆదేశించారు. #AndhraPradesh

Calling for coordinated use of the State's data lake to analyse information across departments and identify gaps in revenue mobilisation, he set March 2027 as the deadline for achieving complete improvements in the functioning of revenue-generating systems.

Mr. Naidu asked departments, including Commercial Taxes, Excise, Mines, Stamps and Registration, Municipal Administration, Panchayat Raj and Forests, to adopt technology-driven monitoring mechanisms. Revenue growth should be tracked continuously from the constituency level to the State level, he said.

The Chief Minister also asked the Stamps and Registration Department to study land market values and registration charges, while directing the Excise Department to ensure end-to-end tracking of liquor from manufacturing to retail sales. The Transport Department was asked to electronically monitor vehicle loads, e-way bills and other relevant parameters.

Officials said tax revenue had increased from ₹53,692 crore during the corresponding period last year to ₹63,796 crore this year, generating an additional ₹10,104 crore. Tax revenue grew by 18.8%, while non-tax revenue registered a growth of 31.3%.
Commercial Taxes revenue rose by 18.3% to ₹38,241 crore, an increase of ₹5,917 crore. GST collections grew by 18.1% to ₹24,073 crore, generating an additional ₹3,694 crore.
Excise revenue increased by ₹3,287 crore, or 19.6%, to ₹20,083 crore. Stamps and Registration revenue rose by 16.6% to ₹8,020 crore, while vehicle tax collections increased by 17.3% to ₹3,649 crore.

fullParagraphs: Following the directive, District Collector informs CMO the action taken against those involved in the illegal activity and measures initiated to prevent recurrence of such incidents

Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has sought a report on the alleged illegal sand mining in the Penna river in Proddatur mandal of Kadapa district and the damage caused to a drinking water pipeline during the activity.
Taking note of media reports on the incident on Wednesday, Mr. Naidu directed the officials to immediately submit a comprehensive explanation.
Following the instructions, the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) sought a report from the Kadapa district administration.

Cases under stringent sections were registered against those responsible for damaging the drinking water pipeline and the tractor owners. Repairs to the damaged pipeline were completed on a war-footing and water supply was restored, he added.

The Collector said the district administration had initiated measures to prevent recurrence of such incidents. Special check-posts were established along the Penna and Chitravathi rivers to curb illegal sand mining and transportation.

District and mandal-level committees were also constituted to monitor mining activities. Village panchayat secretaries and tahsildars of the mandals concerned were instructed to coordinate and prevent illegal transportation through the check-posts, the Collector said, adding that continuous surveillance was arranged along the Penna river.

articles.title: No tampering, violation found at Sheshnag lake: J&K Minister Altaf Kaloo
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: ‘The BRO has not done anything to the lake. The viral video is misleading, as there is a gap of 200-300 ft. between the [pilgrim] track and the lake,’ says J&K Forest Minister Altaf Kaloo

Responding to a viral video that purportedly showed damage caused during an inspection of Sheshnag Lake in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir Forest Minister Altaf Kaloo said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) that a 12-member team of officials had inspected the high-altitude lake and “found no tampering or violations” at the site.

“A team was sent to the spot yesterday [Tuesday] on the directions of the Chief Minister. Later, I was apprised by officials that Sheshnag lake is completely safe. The BRO [Border Roads Organisation] has not done anything to the lake. The viral video is misleading, as there is a gap of 200-300 ft. between the [pilgrim] track and the lake. No tampering has been done. Not a speck of earth has fallen into the lake. It is a sacred, religious place for Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs,” Mr. Kaloo said.

The Minister referred to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by the Omar Abdullah government and the BRO’s Project Beacon in 2025 on the Amarnath route. “An unfortunate eventuality occurred in 2012, and the Supreme Court, while taking cognisance [of it], ordered a 12-ft. track. The current track is in accordance with the SC’s ruling,” he said.

The track underwent a maintenance drive in 2022 after the yatra was over, he said. “The drive is meant to fix broken tiles and edges. We are checking all the parameters of the MoU to ensure they are followed. I wanted to visit the lake but could not because of security reasons. I was told that there was no security ahead,” Mr. Kaloo said.

The team that visited the spot included officials from Environment, Ecology, and Territorial Forests divisions, and the Forest Protection Force, he said. The People’s Democratic Party (PDP) and the BJP were making “a mountain out of a molehill to create an issue for the Uttar Pradesh elections”, the Minister said.

Another leader and legislator of the ruling National Conference (NC), Tanvir Sadiq, said the Omar Abdullah government “will not allow any deviation in the Sheshnag road project and will not allow anyone to play with the environment”. Mr. Abdullah had ordered an environmental assessment of the Sheshnag road project, and assured action in case of any violations, Mr. Sadiq said.

“This project started in 2022. In 2022, the plan was made; in 2023, the MoU was signed; and in 2024, the SC gave its approval. After the 2024 approval, the work started. Where was Mehbooba Mufti sahiba in 2022, 2023, and 2024? Did she not have shoes to go trekking to see this?” Mr. Sadiq said, responding to PDP president Mehbooba Mufti’s allegations on the J&K government signing an MoU with the BRO.
This was a deliberate plan of the BJP and the PDP “to show the whole country that Muslims are against it so that the BJP can sell it not only in Jammu but also in the U.P. elections”, Mr. Sadiq said.
The J&K government was aware of the “importance of the environment and will not allow anyone to play with it”, Mr. Sadiq said.
“At the same time, it will not allow these people to play the Hindu-Muslim card again,” he added.

‘The BRO has not done anything to the lake. The viral video is misleading, as there is a gap of 200-300 ft. between the [pilgrim] track and the lake,’ says J&K Forest Minister Altaf Kaloo

Responding to a viral video that purportedly showed damage caused during an inspection of Sheshnag Lake in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir Forest Minister Altaf Kaloo said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) that a 12-member team of officials had inspected the high-altitude lake and “found no tampering or violations” at the site.

“A team was sent to the spot yesterday [Tuesday] on the directions of the Chief Minister. Later, I was apprised by officials that Sheshnag lake is completely safe. The BRO [Border Roads Organisation] has not done anything to the lake. The viral video is misleading, as there is a gap of 200-300 ft. between the [pilgrim] track and the lake. No tampering has been done. Not a speck of earth has fallen into the lake. It is a sacred, religious place for Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs,” Mr. Kaloo said.

The Minister referred to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by the Omar Abdullah government and the BRO’s Project Beacon in 2025 on the Amarnath route. “An unfortunate eventuality occurred in 2012, and the Supreme Court, while taking cognisance [of it], ordered a 12-ft. track. The current track is in accordance with the SC’s ruling,” he said.

The track underwent a maintenance drive in 2022 after the yatra was over, he said. “The drive is meant to fix broken tiles and edges. We are checking all the parameters of the MoU to ensure they are followed. I wanted to visit the lake but could not because of security reasons. I was told that there was no security ahead,” Mr. Kaloo said.

The team that visited the spot included officials from Environment, Ecology, and Territorial Forests divisions, and the Forest Protection Force, he said. The People’s Democratic Party (PDP) and the BJP were making “a mountain out of a molehill to create an issue for the Uttar Pradesh elections”, the Minister said.

Another leader and legislator of the ruling National Conference (NC), Tanvir Sadiq, said the Omar Abdullah government “will not allow any deviation in the Sheshnag road project and will not allow anyone to play with the environment”. Mr. Abdullah had ordered an environmental assessment of the Sheshnag road project, and assured action in case of any violations, Mr. Sadiq said.

“This project started in 2022. In 2022, the plan was made; in 2023, the MoU was signed; and in 2024, the SC gave its approval. After the 2024 approval, the work started. Where was Mehbooba Mufti sahiba in 2022, 2023, and 2024? Did she not have shoes to go trekking to see this?” Mr. Sadiq said, responding to PDP president Mehbooba Mufti’s allegations on the J&K government signing an MoU with the BRO.

This was a deliberate plan of the BJP and the PDP “to show the whole country that Muslims are against it so that the BJP can sell it not only in Jammu but also in the U.P. elections”, Mr. Sadiq said.

The J&K government was aware of the “importance of the environment and will not allow anyone to play with it”, Mr. Sadiq said.

“At the same time, it will not allow these people to play the Hindu-Muslim card again,” he added.

fullParagraphs: B.C. Indira Reddy, wife of Roads and Buildings Minister B.C. Janardhan Reddy, on Wednesday received her declaration certificate following her unanimous election as sarpanch of Banaganapalle Major Gram Panchayat.

Ms. Indira Reddy received the certificate from election officer Subhashini at a programme held at the Banaganapalle MPDO office. The 20 ward members, who were also elected unanimously, received their declaration certificates. Tanguturi Srinivasulu was unanimously elected Upa-Sarpanch.
Ms. Indira Reddy has been involved in several initiatives focusing on environmental conservation, women’s empowerment and employment opportunities for youth in the Banaganapalle constituency.

Her initiatives include the ‘Haritha Palle’ (Green Village) programme, taken up at a cost of ₹30 lakh, and the provision of monthly nutritional support to 100 pregnant women. She has also launched an initiative to make Banaganapalle plastic-free.

Under the ‘My Banaganapalle – My Health’ initiative, extensive awareness campaigns were conducted against the use of plastic. The initiative has helped the town achieve nearly 80% plastic-free status.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Despite September’s performance, net FDI in the first half of the financial year was more than 20% higher than in the same period last year

Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Bangladesh tightens border security ahead of Hasina's planned return; deploys 108 BGB platoons
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The heightened security comes amid fears that Ms. Hasina's supporters could intensify violence and sabotage in the coming days. Awami League, whose activities have been banned, is promoting a lockdown programme for November 29 and 30 through online platforms, adding to concerns over a possible escalation of tensions

Bangladesh beefed up security across several districts, deploying 108 platoons of border paramilitary forces, including 56 in exiled former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's home district, Gopalganj, as political tensions mount over her planned return next month.

There have been incidents of violence, including arson attacks targeting trains, buses and banks, across Bangladesh in the last many days surrounding the 79-year-old politician's possible return. Ms. Hasina has been staying in India since fleeing Dhaka in August 2024 following a student-led uprising that toppled her government.
Police blamed activists of Awami League and its affiliated organisations for several of the incidents.

The heightened security comes amid fears that Ms. Hasina's supporters could intensify violence and sabotage in the coming days. Awami League, whose activities have been banned, is promoting a lockdown programme for November 29 and 30 through online platforms, adding to concerns over a possible escalation of tensions.

In a press statement on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) announced the deployment of 108 platoons in seven districts "to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and deal with any untoward situation", news portal bdnews24.com reported.
Of them, 56 platoons have been deployed in Gopalganj amid persistent unrest, the BGB said.

Gopalganj, a stronghold of the Awami League, has witnessed incidents of violence, arson and vandalism in recent days. Around 2,000 police personnel and 10 BGB platoons, along with personnel of the Special Response Battalion (SRB), were deployed in the district last week.
According to the BGB statement, 18 platoons have been deployed in Dhaka, six in Narayanganj, 18 in Gazipur, two in Mymensingh, three in Chattogram and one in Cox's Bazar districts.
"In addition, four platoons of BGB members have been kept on alert for deployment," it said.

The deployment has been made on the instructions of the Home Ministry, with BGB personnel coordinating with the respective district administrations and other law enforcement agencies, the Prothom Alo newspaper reported.

articles.title: Execution of proclamation orders against Hafiz Saeed, five other 26/11 accused still awaited
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: A special court issued proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in July this year; the court is currently conducting the trial against handler Abu Jundal

While the trial in the 26/11 terror attacks is on against Zabiuddin Ansari alias Abu Jundal, the handler who taught the 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists Hindi, steps to execute the proclamation orders against six other perpetrators, including Lashkar operatives Hafiz Saeed and Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, are yet to be taken.
A special court issued proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in July this year. The court is currently conducting the trial against Jundal.

In August and September this year, the prosecution told the court that it had requested the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to serve the proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks case. However, the MHA has not responded to the request yet.

Special Public Prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam said that while there has been no development regarding the execution of the proclamation orders issued against the wanted accused, he assured that the perpetrators of the attacks would be punished in India.
"The prosecution will ensure that all those persons who facilitated the dastardly attacks would be punished on Indian soil," Mr. Nikam told PTI .

He said, as per procedure, non-bailable warrants and Interpol Red Corner notices were issued through diplomatic channels against the absconding accused, who are the main perpetrators and conspirators behind the attacks.
"But I am sure that the Pakistan government will not respond as that country continues to be a haven for terrorists," Mr. Nikam said.

The prosecution had in August and September told the court that the MHA was requested to take necessary steps to serve the proclamation orders, through Interpol, against the accused believed to be residing in Pakistan.

Mr. Nikam had then told the court that amid the procedural compliance, the trial against the absconding accused would commence as Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 allows criminal trials in absentia for absconding proclaimed offenders, even where there is no immediate prospect of arrest.

The trial against Jundal, which had been on hold since 2018 pending a petition filed by government authorities over the furnishing of certain documents to the accused, commenced in November last year after clearance from the Bombay High Court.

A special court issued proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in July this year; the court is currently conducting the trial against handler Abu Jundal

While the trial in the 26/11 terror attacks is on against Zabiuddin Ansari alias Abu Jundal, the handler who taught the 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists Hindi, steps to execute the proclamation orders against six other perpetrators, including Lashkar operatives Hafiz Saeed and Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, are yet to be taken.

A special court issued proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in July this year. The court is currently conducting the trial against Jundal.

In August and September this year, the prosecution told the court that it had requested the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to serve the proclamation orders against the six absconding accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks case. However, the MHA has not responded to the request yet.

Special Public Prosecutor Ujjwal Nikam said that while there has been no development regarding the execution of the proclamation orders issued against the wanted accused, he assured that the perpetrators of the attacks would be punished in India.

"The prosecution will ensure that all those persons who facilitated the dastardly attacks would be punished on Indian soil," Mr. Nikam told PTI .

He said, as per procedure, non-bailable warrants and Interpol Red Corner notices were issued through diplomatic channels against the absconding accused, who are the main perpetrators and conspirators behind the attacks.

"But I am sure that the Pakistan government will not respond as that country continues to be a haven for terrorists," Mr. Nikam said.

The prosecution had in August and September told the court that the MHA was requested to take necessary steps to serve the proclamation orders, through Interpol, against the accused believed to be residing in Pakistan.

Mr. Nikam had then told the court that amid the procedural compliance, the trial against the absconding accused would commence as Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 allows criminal trials in absentia for absconding proclaimed offenders, even where there is no immediate prospect of arrest.

The trial against Jundal, which had been on hold since 2018 pending a petition filed by government authorities over the furnishing of certain documents to the accused, commenced in November last year after clearance from the Bombay High Court.

articles.title: Air pollution accelerates dementia by reprogramming brain's immune cells: study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third
Air pollution helps cause dementia by changing the genes that are switched on in microglia, the brain's immune cells, in ways that disrupt their normal functions, a new study has found.
The study, published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation , combined health records from nearly half a million people from the UK Biobank with experiments in mouse models.

"By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain's immune cells," senior author Sanjay Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at the Case Western Reserve University's school of medicine, said.

"These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world's population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it," Rajagopalan said.

Mice were exposed to outdoor Cleveland (US) air for five months. The fine particles in the air, known as particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), were concentrated to levels similar to those found in the world's most polluted cities.

Otherwise healthy mice developed memory problems, a leaky blood-brain barrier and brain inflammation. Their brains also showed a lower chemical balance reflecting its energy status and ability to withstand injury and disease.
The mice's brains also showed an increased death of newborn neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's centre for learning and memory.
The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third.
Further, in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer's, air pollution caused the same harm and also sped up amyloid plaque buildup -- a hallmark of the neurodegenerative disease.

The authors wrote: "These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure."

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 25 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 4 Min Read

📰 Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: CPI inflation peaked to 6.1 % (y-o-y) in October 2026 from 5.5% in September 2026, slightly above the upper tolerance level of 6%–last observed in October 2024.
High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.

Industrial facilities in the city of Syzran, in Russia’s Samara region, came ‌under Ukrainian drone attack overnight, and one person was killed ‌in a Ukrainian drone strike on ‌the ⁠regional capital, Samara, local authorities ⁠said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Syzran and Samara, located on the Volga River, host three major oil refineries. According ​to unverified ‌reports on social media, at least two of them, the Syzran and Kuibyshev oil refineries, were attacked. Reuters could ‌not independently verify that.

“There are consequences ‘on the ‌ground’ that you yourselves can see. But let me remind you that you must not play into the enemy’s hands. Do not publish any photos or videos showing the aftermath ‌of the attack,” he wrote on VKontakte, ​Russia’s Facebook equivalent.

Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries subsided somewhat after U.S. ⁠President Donald Trump’s mid-October declaration of an ⁠energy ceasefire. But they have picked up again sharply since the ‌end of last month.
Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged retaliation for ​the Ukrainian strikes on Tuesday (November 24).

articles.title: MEA separates Sheikh Hasina’s plans to return to Bangladesh from issue of extradition
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: ‘The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,’ MEA’s official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said

The return of the deposed former Prime Minister of Bangladesh Sheikh Hasina, using a “travel document” to her country and the process of her extradition from India to Bangladesh were two separate issues, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026). Speaking at the bi-weekly press briefing, the MEA’s official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal made the distinction, while expressing concern over the prevailing law and order situation in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh’s request for Ms. Hasina’s extradition, made during the tenure of the interim government under Prof. Mohammed Yunus, is “being examined in line with our established processes”, Mr. Jaiswal said. Dhaka, in recent weeks, has talked about getting Ms. Hasina through an “acceptable prisoner exchange process”. Ms. Hasina had earlier this month requested the High Commission of Bangladesh, through a U.K.-based law firm, to issue her a fresh Bangladesh passport so that she could return home. Mr. Jaiswal said her plans to return to her country were separate from India extraditing her to Bangladesh.

“The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,” Mr. Jaiswal said, adding that the issue of her return was a matter “between the former Prime Minister and the Bangladesh government”.

Ms. Hasina’s supporters from the Awami League have been agitating in her party’s strongholds in places, including Gopalganj and Narail, where the party’s workers have been targeted by law enforcement authorities. “We understandably are concerned at the incidents of violence against minorities in Bangladesh. We urge the government of Bangladesh to thoroughly investigate these incidents and bring the perpetrators to justice,” Mr. Jaiswal said.

articles.title: Great Nicobar Island project: Final Calcutta High Court hearing deferred as Centre seeks to file affidavit, objections
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Centre argues that the FRA is not implemented in the A&NI, objects to some petitions claiming that they should be heard by the NGT or SC; next hearing posted for January 13, 2027; court to hear Attorney General of India on January 22

The Calcutta High Court’s final hearing in a batch of petitions alleging forest rights violations in diverting forest land for the Union government’s ₹92,000 crore Great Nicobar Island (GNI) project was deferred again on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), after the Centre sought time to file another affidavit and some documents on the question of tribal rights.

The Centre argued that the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, is not implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (A&NI), which the petitioners rebutted by noting that the Islands administration has already issued a certificate claiming that FRA rights have been settled, which is what is being challenged.

The High Court Bench, led by Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge, has now posted the hearing for the batch of petitions on January 13, 2027, when the court is also expected to begin hearing a petition that specifically challenged the A&NI administration’s orders claiming that all provisions of the FRA had been complied with in diverting 121 sq.km. for the GNI project.
This comes after the Centre told the Supreme Court in October this year that it would be best if the “High Court is requested to consider and decide all such cases at the earliest”.

On Wednesday, when the Calcutta High Court was about to start the final hearing in these petitions as per the orders of the Supreme Court, Additional Solicitor General (ASG) of India Vikramjit Banerjee submitted that the Centre wished to once again raise preliminary objections on the maintainability of some of the petitions. Further, on the question of tribal rights, the ASG said the Centre wished to submit one more affidavit with some additional documents. Attorney General for India, R. Venkatramani, also appeared before the High Court on Wednesday.
Profile: The Great Nicobar project | Between the sea and the state

The Centre’s lawyers argued that on the question of the FRA, the law that is alleged to have been violated, it has been the historical stand of the Union government, across administrations, that the FRA need not be pursued in A&NI because the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, was already operational there.

In response, the petitioner’s counsel pointed out that the A&NI administration had explicitly issued a certificate saying that the rights of local tribespeople had been settled under the FRA and that this certificate is what has been challenged.

Further, the Centre submitted that it would like to continue arguing on the maintainability of two more petitions tagged as part of the same issue, noting that these two petitions dealt with matters that should be brought either before the National Green Tribunal or the Supreme Court.
The petitioner’s counsel objected to this and clarified that these two petitions specifically deal with orders that reduce the buffer zones for two specific National Parks on Great Nicobar Island.
